rich_summary: Sringin tells his father, the sage Samika, that in anger he has cursed King Parikshit: within seven days the serpent Takshaka will kill him. Samika rebukes his son, teaching that ascetics must practice restraint and forgiveness. He argues that kings, even when they err, uphold social order, protect religious rites, and sustain the cosmic cycle that benefits all. Anger, he warns, destroys the spiritual merit gained through penance. Although the curse cannot be undone because of Sringin’s truthful power, Samika compassionately sends his disciple Gaurmukha to warn the king. When Parikshit hears the message, he feels deep remorse—not primarily for his impending death, but for the disrespect he showed the silent sage. The passage contrasts youthful wrath with mature wisdom and highlights repentance, duty, and the fragile balance between spiritual power and moral restraint.

highlight_spans.why: The moment Sringin declares the fatal curse on King Parikshit and foretells Takshaka’s role.
Samika’s warning about Dharma and the responsibility to forgive rulers establishes the moral framework of the chapter.
Samika’s teaching that anger destroys the merit of asceticism emphasizes the spiritual theme of self‑control.
Parikshit’s reaction of remorse highlights his moral awareness and emotional turning point.

top_scenes.scene_text: Young ascetic Sringin, blazing with anger in a forest hermitage, pronounces the deadly curse that the serpent king Takshaka will kill Parikshit in seven days.
The calm sage Samika instructs his furious son beneath forest trees, urging forgiveness and warning that anger destroys ascetic merit.
In a royal court, the ascetic messenger Gaurmukha solemnly delivers the curse to King Parikshit, who sits surrounded by ministers and falls into remorse.
